messages.content:
You are checking one scene of a novel for one specific continuity error.

The book had already established this, earlier or elsewhere:
- (the-governors-vigil) "Sera Holdt. First floor, nine years."

A past rewrite of this scene contradicted it. The error looked like this:
- (haddons-reckoning) "Sera Holdt, sixty-eight. Upper floors."
(Summary: Sera Holdt lived on the first floor in the-governors-vigil but on the upper floors in haddons-reckoning.)

Here is a NEW draft of the same scene:
<scene>
He heard the runner before he saw him, the quick uneven clatter of boots on the grating three sections down, the rhythm of a man who did not run often and was running now. Haddon set down his wrench on the lip of the manifold housing and wiped his palm on his apron. The brass under his hand was warm. It was always warm this deep, and he had spent twenty years not asking how warm was too warm.

The runner came around the bend red-faced, one hand braced on the pipe rail. A Gallery boy, sixteen maybe, name Haddon did not have.

"Southern Basin," the boy got out. "Junction failure. Fenwick Row South. Two dead. Vael's on scene."

Haddon did not move for a moment. The manifold housing beside him ticked as it cooled, the slow metallic settling he had come to use as a clock. He had reset this housing at dawn. It had failed by midday. He had reset it again. Six hours, give or take, and the gauge would climb back into the red and he would climb back up here and turn the valve and log it within tolerance and go home.

"Compensatory load?" he said. Flat. The word a tradesman used.

The boy blinked. "Chief said tell you. That's all I got."

"Two dead."

"That's what the runner from Fenwick said." The boy's throat worked. "Said one was a kid."

Haddon picked the wrench back up. He did not need it. He held it the way another man might hold a railing. "Go tell the chief I heard."

The boy went.

He finished the housing. That was the part he would think about later, in the dark, when his wife was asleep and he was not. He finished the housing. He seated the gasket and ran the flange bolts down in sequence and checked the gauge and watched the needle settle where it was supposed to settle, and he wrote in the log book, in his own hand, *Junction 14 manifold reseated, pressure within tolerance,* and the ink dried on the page while he watched it.

Then he climbed the ladder out of the active galleries and told Fen Aldric, who kept the shift desk, that he was stepping out.

"How long?"

"Don't know."

Fen looked at him. Fen had worked the Basin longer than Haddon had, and there were things Fen did not ask about, which was why Fen still worked the shift desk. "You all right?"

"I need to step out," Haddon said, and left.

---

Fenwick Row South sat where the old market hall used to be, a square of narrow terrace houses stacked four high against the caldera wall. Haddon had grown up eleven streets over. He knew the grade of it, the way the lane dropped toward the drainage channel, the smell of coal smoke and mineral water that never fully cleared no matter the hour.

There was a crowd. There was always a crowd at a rupture, pressed back behind a rope the rescue crew had strung across the lane. Steam still hung over the square, thinning gold where the amber gaslight caught it. The front of the third house had come apart. Not fallen. Come apart, the stone face sheared off clean where the pressure had found the seam in the old First Expansion flange and widened it into a mouth.

He stood at the rope with his apron still on and his wrench still in his hand because he had forgotten he was holding it.

A woman from the upper floors sat on a doorstep across the lane, a blanket over her shoulders, saying a name over and over to a neighbor who kept hold of her arm. A small girl in a nightdress stood apart from everyone, barefoot on the wet stone, watching the rescue crew the way children watch things they have not yet been told to understand.

The crew chief came down off the rubble pile, saw the apron, saw the wrench, and read him for what he was.

"You Gallery?"

Haddon nodded.

"Then you can tell me why a sealed-off junction four levels down blew the face off a house up here." The man's own face was grey with dust. "Because I can't. My boys can't. Nobody can tell me a damned thing except it wasn't supposed to be able to happen."

"Who's dead," Haddon said.

The chief wiped his mouth. "Old woman upstairs. Holdt. Sixty-eight. Lived here forty years, the neighbor says." He jerked his chin at the ruined ground floor. "And a boy. Erdel. Seven. He was down here with his mother and she got out and he didn't."

Sera Holdt, sixty-eight. Tam Erdel, seven. Haddon stood very still and the numbers he had been reading off gauges for two years, the variance figures, the tolerated drift, acquired names and ages and a street he had walked as a child, and he understood, with the slow full weight of a flange giving way, that the arithmetic had always been this and he had only kept it folded small enough to carry.

Vael was there. Haddon saw him near the breach, crouched, a journal open on his knee, writing. His hands were steady on the page. Haddon knew the stillness in those hands. He had seen it in his own father, who had reset failing valves in the First Expansion galleries until the day one did not wait for him to finish, and who had come home grey like that chief was grey and had said nothing at supper and had never said much again. His father had taught him the word *tolerance*. His father had taught him that a man did his work and did not reach past the end of his wrench.

He did not go to Vael. There was nothing he could say to Vael that would not be a confession, and he was not ready, standing in that lane, to make it.

He saw the shoes before he left.

They were on the ground near the rope, a little pair, set side by side where someone had pulled them off a child who had no more use for them. Leather, scuffed pale at the toes the way all boys' shoes scuffed, from kicking at steps and walls and anything a foot could reach. One lace was untied. Nobody had thought to tie it, or had not had the heart, and it lay there in the wet with its small frayed end in the runoff.

Haddon looked at the shoes for a long time. Then he turned and went back up the hill, and his own boots were very loud on the stone, and he did not finish any thought he started the whole way back.

---

The envelope was on the shift desk when he returned. Fen was not there. The lamp was turned low. The thing sat under a flange washer someone had used to weight it, plain paper, no seal, his name on the front in a hand he did not know and recognized anyway as the kind of hand a man uses when he does not want his own found on a thing.

He opened it.

*Tonight. Third watch. Southern access corridor. Instruments will be in position. The core. Full neutralization.*

No name. There did not need to be a name. He had been receiving instructions without names for two years, and he had learned their grammar, the way they never asked for a thing outright, the way they described a state of affairs that would be improved by his attention. He knew what *the core* meant. He had suspected what was down there in the sealed galleries for longer than he had let himself frame the suspicion in words. He had logged the manifold reseated and written *within tolerance* while that sentence became a different kind of sentence, became the small rehearsed language by which he had let a boy's shoes end up untied in a gutter.

He read it again. *Full neutralization.*

He had told himself, for two years, that the drift was mechanical. That the eastern draw was old pipe settling, the compensatory load a quirk of a system too big for any one man to hold in his head. He had told himself that the reports Vael filed were a careful man seeing patterns in noise. He had told himself a great many things, in the careful self-deceiving voice a man learns, and the voice had held because the cost had always stayed abstract, a figure in a column, a variance within tolerance.

Sera Holdt, sixty-eight. Tam Erdel, seven.

He struck a match and held the corner of the note to it and watched it curl and blacken and drop into the tin pan he kept on the desk for exactly this, the way he had burned a dozen such notes before, the ash no different from any other ash. The flame reached his fingers and he let it, a half-second past when he should have let go, and then he dropped the last of it and pressed his thumb against the heat on his skin.

Fen Aldric came back in from the corridor with two mugs, saw the pan, saw Haddon's face, and set the mugs down slow.

"Southern flange," Fen said, because he had to say something. "Failed about forty minutes after you left. Same as the last six."

"Same failure mode?"

"Same failure mode."

Haddon looked at the smear of ash in the tin. Six-hour cycle. It would climb into the red again before midnight, and a man would be sent down to reset it, and it would hold for six hours, and the whole patient dying system would go on being reset by men who wrote *within tolerance* in good clear hands. And tonight, at third watch, instruments would be in position in the southern access corridor, and whatever had been holding this city balanced for longer than any of them had been alive would be taken apart for good, and the resets would stop, because there would be nothing left to reset.

"Get Orath," he said.

Fen did not move. "Haddon."

"Get Orath. And the night crew. Full shift. I need them here by third watch."

"That's not your shift to call. The order comes from—"

"I know where the order comes from." Haddon stood. His knees did not feel like his. "Get them. Tell them it's the eastern galleries. Tell them to bring cutters and lamps and every length of brace line in the shop. Tell them Breck said."

Fen stood holding the edge of the desk, reading him the way the crew chief had read him, and whatever he found there was enough. He went to the speaking tube and worked the whistle and bent to it. "Orath. Shift desk. Night crew, full compliment, third watch, no excuses." He straightened. "You want Lonn and Cade too?"

"Everyone." Haddon crossed to the tool wall and took down a bag and began loading it, by feel, the way he had done ten thousand times, bracket wrenches and the long bar and the cutters, his hands steady now that there was something for them to do. "Everyone who'll come."

"And when they ask who ordered it against the Gallery?"

Haddon pulled the bag's strap over his shoulder. The manifold housing four levels down ticked toward its sixth hour, somewhere under his feet, and would climb, and no one would be sent to reset it tonight.

He picked up his wrench off the desk where he'd set it down.

"Tell them I did."

</scene>

Does the new draft make the same error — does it assert something that contradicts what was established, in the way described? A draft that simply leaves the fact out does not make the error.

Answer with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"verdict": "reintroduced" | "consistent" | "not_present", "evidence": "<verbatim sentence from the new draft that decides it, or empty for not_present>"}

"reintroduced": the new draft contradicts the established fact.
"consistent": the new draft states the fact and agrees with what was established.
"not_present": the new draft does not touch the fact either way.

content.text: {"verdict": "reintroduced", "evidence": "The chief wiped his mouth. \"Old woman upstairs. Holdt. Sixty-eight. Lived here forty years, the neighbor says.\""}
